An exclamation is a word, phrase, or sentence that bursts out of a person because of a strong, sudden feeling. When something shocks you, thrills you, hurts you, angers you, or overwhelms you — and words escape you instantly and forcefully — those words are an exclamation.

It is not a calm, thought-out statement. It's an emotional outburst in word form.

You touch a hot pan. You don't pause and say, "I seem to be experiencing pain." You shout — "Ouch!" That is an exclamation.

You open a gift and it's exactly what you wanted. You cry out — "Oh my goodness! Yes!" Those are exclamations.

A friend tells you the most shocking news you've ever heard. You gasp — "I can't believe it!" Also an exclamation.

In every case, the feeling came first. The words followed instantly, driven by that feeling.

Exclamations come in different sizes:

A single word: "Wow!" — "No!" — "Ouch!" — "Incredible!" — "Hurray!"

A short phrase: "Oh my!" — "How awful!" — "Good grief!" — "What a shame!"

A full sentence: "This is unbelievable!" — "How kind you are!" — "I had no idea!"

What all of them share is the same essential quality: they are pulled out by strong emotion, not careful reasoning.
The four sentence types — where exclamation fits

English sentences fall into four types. Knowing these will sharpen your understanding of what makes an exclamation distinct:

  1. Statement — calmly tells you something. → "The game is over."
  2. Question — asks something. → "Is the game over?"
  3. Command — tells someone to do something. → "End the game."
  4. Exclamation — expresses strong feeling. → "The game is finally over!" / "What a game that was!"

An exclamation is the only type whose entire purpose is to release an emotion. It doesn't primarily give information, ask something, or instruct — it simply expresses.

The noun "exclamation" is very commonly used in the pattern "an exclamation of [emotion]":

  • "She let out an exclamation of surprise."
  • "He gave a sharp exclamation of pain."
  • "There were exclamations of joy from the crowd."
  • "I heard an exclamation of disbelief from across the room."

Notice that the word "exclamation" alone doesn't tell you which emotion — only that some strong emotion was behind it. The phrase that follows ("of surprise", "of joy") specifies it.

The punctuation symbol ! is called the exclamation mark (also "exclamation point" in American English). It was created precisely to signal that a word or sentence is an exclamation — to tell the reader: this is to be read with force and feeling, not in a flat tone.

"Help!" — the mark shows urgency and fear. Without it: "Help" — suddenly flat and strange.

"That's incredible!" — the mark captures the speaker's genuine amazement.

That said, in casual and informal writing today, people often use ! simply to sound enthusiastic or friendly, even in ordinary sentences. But the mark's primary, defining purpose is to signal a true exclamation.

In grammar, a special group of words called interjections exist solely to express emotion. They have no grammatical job in a sentence — they simply burst in:

Wow! — Ouch! — Ah! — Oh! — Ugh! — Phew! — Hurray! — Alas! — Yikes!

Every interjection is an exclamation, but not every exclamation is an interjection. "Ouch!" is a one-word interjection. "I cannot believe how talented she is!" is a full-sentence exclamation — not an interjection, but still very much an exclamation.

In everyday speech, we exclaim constantly and naturally, without thinking.

In written stories and novels, exclamations bring characters to life. When a character exclaims, the reader feels their emotion. A character who only ever speaks in calm statements feels distant. Exclamations make dialogue feel human and real.

However — and this is important — skilled writers use exclamations sparingly. If every sentence has an exclamation mark, nothing feels special or urgent. The power of an exclamation comes from contrast: it stands out against calmer sentences. Overusing it is one of the most common mistakes in writing.
The complete picture in one place

An exclamation is a word, phrase, or sentence that expresses a strong emotion — surprise, pain, joy, anger, fear, excitement, admiration, disgust, or relief — spontaneously and with force. It is one of the four types of sentences in English, and the only one whose sole purpose is emotional expression. The exclamation mark (!) is its written signal. Words like "Wow!", "Ouch!", "Alas!" are single-word exclamations called interjections — the purest and most naked form of exclamation, carrying emotion with nothing else attached.
